query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A combined computational–experimental protocol that couples high-temperature thermodynamic integration via atomistic simulations (e.g., hybrid Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics calibrated using local distortions and chemical short‐range order data) with in situ calorimetric measurements can rapidly and accurately determine the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and select liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across single‐phase high‐entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: High‐entropy alloys in a well‐defined single-phase state (e.g., FCC solid solution) with carefully controlled compositions to minimize secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Apply a hybrid methodology that uses calibrated atomistic simulations to compute fusion properties (leveraging local lattice distortion and configurational entropy estimates) and validate/adjust these predictions with high-temperature differential scanning calorimetry and dilatometry.
generation.conditions: The approach applies to HEAs with moderate compositional complexity where chemical short‐range order and local atomic distortions have been characterized; experiments are conducted under controlled atmospheres to prevent oxidation and at heating rates that allow equilibrium to be approached.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic distortions and chemical short‐range order, which influence both the fusion thermodynamics and the effective configurational entropy of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The coupling of computational estimates of free energy changes (including fusion enthalpy, entropy, and volume change) with experimental validation exploits the fact that local bonding variations (as seen in prior work on HEA systems) correlate with macroscopic melting and liquid-state properties. Adjusting simulation parameters with in-situ measurements minimizes errors stemming from the intrinsic configurational entropy of high-entropy alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method is expected to yield fusion property predictions with less than about 5–10% deviation from direct experimental determinations. It will efficiently map melting temperatures and related thermodynamic quantities across the high-entropy alloy family and demonstrate sensitivity to compositional adjustments.
generation.baseline: Conventional differential scanning calorimetry or high-temperature measurements without simulation guidance, which often lack efficiency or fail to capture full configurational complexities.
generation.boundary: Applicability is limited to single-phase HEAs with well-characterized local structures; multi-phase systems or alloys with extreme chemical segregation may fall outside the effective range.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative accuracy (targeting a 5–10% error range) is contingent upon the quality of the simulation potentials and calibration accuracy of the experimental setup; capturing the full effect of configurational entropy in highly disordered systems may introduce additional uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative set of single-phase HEAs covering a range of compositions. Use the hybrid computational model to predict melting temperature, fused enthalpy, fused entropy, and volume change at melting. Independently measure these properties using high-temperature differential scanning calorimetry and dilatometry under identical conditions. Compare the predicted and experimental values.
measurements: Fusion enthalpy and entropy via integrated heat flow from DSC data
Volume change at melting via high-temperature dilatometry or in-situ synchrotron measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If more than 50% of the tested HEAs show deviations exceeding 10% between predicted and measured values for any of the fusion properties, the proposed hybrid approach would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
How Atomic Bonding Plays the Hardness Behavior in the Al–Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni High Entropy Family

Abstract: AbstractA systematic study on a face‐centered cubic‐based compositionally complex alloy system Al–Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni in its single‐phase state is carried out, where a mother senary compound Al8Co17Cr17Cu8Fe17Ni33 and five of its suballoys, obtained by removing one element at a time, are investigated and exhaustively analyzed determining the contribution of each alloying element in the solid solution. The senary and the quinaries are compared using experimental techniques including X‐ray absorption spectroscopy, X‐ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and first principles hybrid Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations. Chemical short‐range order and bond length distances have been determined both at the experimental and computational level. Electronic structure and local atomic distortions up to 5.2 Å have been correlated to the microhardness values.
